Nixie wasn't designed with system-wide use in mind. The reason you get the errors in Home Manager is due to a quirk with the way rootless Nix (and by extension Nixie) works, in that the `nix` command isn't "installed" in the chroot environment.

You can add a few lines to your `.profile` to zip your entire session in `bwrap` with the `/nix` directory at root, then install Nix the usual way, but then suid binaries won't work.

Nixie being designed to work in a per-project ecosystem, where whole-session or whole-system management isn't required, this issue is currently out of scope.

In the future, I could build upon Nixie to enable session-wide installs (such as hooking into profile generation to provide redirectors in `$PATH`), after all most of the required tech is already in Nixie.


In the mean time I'm of the opinion that Nix is best enjoyed when installed across the system. Quite a few features (like multi-machine builds and `result` links) don't really work when running sandboxed, not to mention system utilities installed through Nix wouldn't work.

If you are interested in implementing a session manager using Nixie, here's a couple pointers:

- Nix loves symlinks. When you "install" a program using Nix, you actually tell Nix to rebuild the profile (which is also a derivation) with the new package in the list. A profile is an overlay of package layouts with symbolic links pointing to their real paths, as a quick `ls -l ~/.nix-profile/bin` will show you.
- Nix and everything it does rely on the `/nix` directory existing at system root, and therein lies the whole issue with developing Nixie in the first place. Root directories (usually) require root privileges, so the only other way is a container or sandbox. Outside the sandbox though, all profiles, result links and programs will break due to the missing path.
- Nix LOVES symlinks. You'll find symlinks pointing to other symlinks in the store, so you absolutely have to have a way to recursively resolve all of them when the sandbox isn't there. Just pointing to the real store may not be enough, as evidenced by the complexity of [`fakedir`](https://github.com/nixie-dev/fakedir)

I'm thinking hooking into profile generation, and rewriting the links to point to the "real" Nix store (for files) or to the wrapper script (for binaries).

If your system isn't running OpenSSL (maybe it uses LibreSSL?) set `NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE` in the environment to point to your `ca_certificates` bundle. Please share details about what operating system you are running Nixie on.

The issue should not occur on macOS as Nixie sets it to the macOS bundle file, which worked in my testing.

Hello!

I appreciate the contribution! Unfortunately, `nixie for` relies on the [template system](https://github.com/nixie-dev/templates), which is untested and whose design is not yet finalised. I would much rather leave the `nixie for` subcommand unpopulated until I am ready to fully implement project templates in one go.

I'll try and stub the command in a clearer way.

The tests boil down to “simple NixOS config” + “successive shell commands” and could be made generic using a guest unit test framework.
Remaining issue is quality of log outputs in NixOS test runner.

Update! Cachix now serves `zstd` archives even if `xz` was explicitly set on the project page. It looks as though I'd have to ship `zstd` in the script tarball itself.
The reference `zstd` is rather large at 1.1MB and I don't want to hard-dep on a relatively new tool.

On the other hand the source build process is an upstanding citizen of pure, dependency-less C. 10 megabytes of it. Nah.
